tests.title: OS Practice — Memory & Virtual Memory
tests.subject: Computer Science

questions.question_en: An address generated by the CPU while a program is running is called a:
questions.explanation_en: The CPU always generates logical (virtual) addresses. The address actually seen by the memory unit, after translation, is the physical address. A frame address and a disk address belong to physical memory and the backing store, not to the CPU's view.

questions.question_en: Which hardware device maps virtual addresses to physical addresses at run time?
questions.explanation_en: The memory-management unit (MMU) translates every logical address into a physical address while the program runs, for example by adding a relocation register or looking up a page table. A DMA controller moves I/O data, and the program counter only holds the address of the next instruction.

questions.question_en: With dynamic relocation, the relocation (base) register holds 24000. The CPU generates logical address 735. Which physical address is accessed?
questions.explanation_en: The MMU adds the relocation register to every logical address: physical = 24000 + 735 = 24735. The user program only ever sees logical addresses from 0 upward; it never sees 24735.

questions.question_en: Memory has five fixed partitions of 150 KB, 350 KB, 220 KB, 500 KB and 280 KB (in this order). A process of 210 KB arrives. Under the best-fit strategy, which partition does it get?
questions.explanation_en: Best fit chooses the smallest partition that is large enough. Partitions that fit 210 KB are 350, 220, 500 and 280 KB; the smallest is 220 KB (only 10 KB left over). First fit would take 350 KB and worst fit would take 500 KB.

questions.question_en: Fixed partitions of 150 KB, 350 KB, 220 KB, 500 KB and 280 KB (in this order) each hold one process. Processes P1 = 200 KB, P2 = 330 KB, P3 = 480 KB and P4 = 140 KB arrive in that order. Using worst fit, which process must wait?
questions.explanation_en: Worst fit gives each process the largest free partition. P1 (200) takes 500 KB, P2 (330) takes 350 KB, then P3 (480) finds only 150, 220 and 280 KB free, so it must wait. P4 (140) takes 280 KB. Best fit would have placed all four (220, 350, 500, 150).

questions.question_en: Fixed partitions of 150 KB, 350 KB, 220 KB, 500 KB and 280 KB (in this order) each hold one process. Processes of 120 KB, 300 KB and 260 KB arrive in that order. Using first fit, which partition does the 260 KB process get?
questions.explanation_en: First fit scans from the start and takes the first free partition that is big enough. 120 KB goes to 150 KB, 300 KB goes to 350 KB, and for 260 KB the scan skips 220 KB (too small) and stops at 500 KB. Best fit would have chosen 280 KB instead.

questions.question_en: Memory that is wasted inside an allocated block, because the block given to a process is larger than what it requested, is called:
questions.explanation_en: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated partition or page (for example, the unused part of a process's last page). External fragmentation is free memory split into small holes between allocations. Compaction is a remedy, and thrashing is excessive paging.

questions.question_en: Compaction shuffles memory contents to place all free memory together in one large block. Which statement about it is correct?

options.en: It removes thrashing and needs extra frames for every process
It removes internal fragmentation and needs static relocation at load time
It removes external fragmentation and needs dynamic relocation at run time
It removes page faults and needs a larger TLB in the MMU

questions.explanation_en: Compaction solves external fragmentation by moving processes so that the scattered holes merge into one block. It is possible only if relocation is dynamic (done at execution time), because moved processes need new base addresses. It does nothing for internal fragmentation.

questions.question_en: A system uses 32-bit logical addresses and a page size of 8 KB. How many bits are used for the page number and for the page offset?
questions.explanation_en: Page size 8 KB = 2^13 bytes, so the offset needs 13 bits. The remaining 32 − 13 = 19 bits form the page number, giving 2^19 pages. The 20/12 split would be for 4 KB pages.

questions.question_en: Physical memory is 256 MB and the frame size is 4 KB. How many frames are there, and how many bits does a physical address need?
questions.explanation_en: 256 MB = 2^28 bytes, so a physical address needs 28 bits. Number of frames = 2^28 / 2^12 = 2^16 = 65,536. Of the 28 bits, 16 select the frame and 12 give the offset.

questions.question_en: A system has a 32-bit logical address, a page size of 16 KB and a page-table entry of 4 bytes. What is the size of a single-level page table for one process?
questions.explanation_en: Number of pages = 2^32 / 2^14 = 2^18 entries. Table size = 2^18 × 4 bytes = 2^20 bytes = 1 MB. With 4 KB pages it would have been 2^20 × 4 = 4 MB.

questions.question_en: A TLB lookup takes 10 ns and a main-memory access takes 100 ns. The TLB hit ratio is 90%. What is the effective memory-access time with paging?
questions.explanation_en: On a hit: 10 + 100 = 110 ns. On a miss: 10 + 100 (page table) + 100 (data) = 210 ns. EAT = 0.9 × 110 + 0.1 × 210 = 99 + 21 = 120 ns. Without a TLB every access would take 200 ns.

questions.question_en:
Segment table:
Segment | Base | Limit
0 | 2000 | 500
1 | 5200 | 300
2 | 800 | 700
3 | 3600 | 1000
What physical address corresponds to the logical address (segment 3, offset 845)?
questions.explanation_en: The offset 845 is less than segment 3's limit of 1000, so the address is legal. Physical address = base + offset = 3600 + 845 = 4445. A trap would occur only if the offset were 1000 or more.

questions.question_en: Which technique lets a process execute even when it is not completely in main memory, so that programs can be larger than the physical RAM?
questions.explanation_en: Virtual memory separates logical memory from physical memory: only the needed parts of a program are kept in RAM and the rest stays on disk. This gives the illusion of a very large main memory. Cache only speeds up access, and spooling is for I/O devices.

questions.question_en: In a pure demand-paging system, when is a page brought into main memory?

options.en: Only when it is referenced during execution
When the process is first created
All pages are loaded when the program starts

questions.explanation_en: Demand paging uses a lazy pager: a page is loaded only when it is actually needed. Pages that are never touched are never loaded, which saves memory and I/O. Loading every page at start is ordinary swapping, not demand paging.

questions.question_en: A page fault occurs when a running process:

options.en: References a page that is already in a frame
Finds the page number in the TLB
Finishes executing the last page of its code
References a page that is marked invalid (not in memory)

questions.explanation_en: If the page-table entry for the referenced page has its valid–invalid bit set to invalid because the page is on disk, the hardware traps to the OS; this trap is a page fault. A page already in a frame or found in the TLB causes no fault.

questions.question_en: While the OS services a page fault, which of these steps is performed LAST?

options.en: Find a free frame for the missing page
Check the internal table to see if the reference was valid
Restart the instruction that was interrupted by the trap
Schedule a disk read of the page into the frame

questions.explanation_en: The order is: check the internal table for a valid reference, find a free frame, schedule a disk read into it, update the tables when the read finishes, and finally restart the instruction that caused the trap. The process then continues as if the page had always been in memory.

questions.question_en: Memory-access time is 100 ns and servicing a page fault takes 10 ms. If the page-fault rate is 0.0002, what is the effective access time?
questions.explanation_en: EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × fault time = 0.9998 × 100 ns + 0.0002 × 10,000,000 ns = 99.98 + 2000 = 2099.98 ns ≈ 2.1 µs. Even one fault in 5000 accesses makes memory about 21 times slower.

questions.question_en: Using FIFO page replacement with 3 frames (initially empty), how many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3, 1, 0, 5, 3, 6?
questions.explanation_en: Frames after each fault: 1; 1,3; 1,3,0; (3 hit); 3,0,5; 0,5,6; 5,6,3; 6,3,1; 3,1,0; 1,0,5; 0,5,3; 5,3,6. Only the second reference to 3 is a hit, so there are 12 − 1 = 11 faults.

questions.question_en: Using LRU page replacement with 3 frames (initially empty), how many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3, 1, 0, 5, 3, 6?
questions.explanation_en: 1, 3, 0 fault; 3 hits; 5 replaces 1 (least recent); 6 replaces 0; 3 hits; 1 replaces 5; 0 replaces 6; 5 replaces 3; 3 replaces 1; 6 replaces 0. Hits are the two references to 3 at positions 4 and 7, so faults = 12 − 2 = 10.

questions.question_en: Using the Optimal page-replacement algorithm with 3 frames (initially empty), how many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3, 1, 0, 5, 3, 6?
questions.explanation_en: 1, 3, 0 fault (3); 3 hits. 5 replaces 0, whose next use is farthest (4); 6 replaces 5 (5); 3 and 1 hit. 0 replaces 1, never used again (6); 5 replaces 0, never used again (7); 3 and 6 hit. Total = 7 faults, against 10 for LRU and 11 for FIFO.

questions.question_en: Using FIFO page replacement with 4 frames (initially empty), how many page faults occur for the reference string 2, 4, 1, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, 2, 1, 5, 3?
questions.explanation_en: 2, 4, 1 fault (3); 4 hits; 3 faults (4: frames 2, 4, 1, 3); 2 hits; 5 replaces 2, the oldest (5); 4 hits; 2 replaces 4 (6: frames 1, 3, 5, 2); 1, 5 and 3 all hit. Total = 6 faults.

questions.question_en: Using LRU page replacement with 4 frames (initially empty), how many page faults occur for the reference string 2, 4, 1, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, 2, 1, 5, 3?
questions.explanation_en: 2, 4, 1, 3 fault (4); 4 and 2 hit; 5 replaces 1, the least recently used (5); 4 and 2 hit; 1 replaces 3 (6); 5 hits; 3 replaces 4 (7). Total = 7 faults; here LRU does one worse than FIFO (6).

questions.question_en: Using the Optimal page-replacement algorithm with 4 frames (initially empty), how many page faults occur for the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1, 2, 6, 1, 2, 3, 4?
questions.explanation_en: 1, 2, 3, 4 fault (4). 5 replaces 4, whose next use is farthest away (5). 1 and 2 hit. 6 replaces 5, which is never used again (6). 1, 2 and 3 hit. 4 faults (7). FIFO and LRU both give 10 faults on this string.

questions.question_en: For the reference string 4, 3, 2, 1, 4, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 5 under FIFO replacement, how many page faults occur with 3 frames and with 4 frames respectively?
questions.explanation_en: With 3 frames FIFO gives 9 faults, but with 4 frames it gives 10. More frames causing more faults is Belady's anomaly, which FIFO can show. LRU on the same string gives 10 and then 8, falling as frames increase.

questions.question_en: Using LRU with 3 frames (initially empty), what is the hit ratio for the reference string 7, 2, 7, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4, 7, 2?
questions.explanation_en: 7, 2 fault; 7 hits; 3 faults; 2 hits; 5 replaces 7; 3 hits; 4 replaces 2; 7 replaces 5; 2 replaces 3. Hits = 3 of 10 references, so the hit ratio is 3/10 = 30% (7 faults).

questions.question_en: A reference string of 20 references contains exactly 6 distinct pages. With 8 frames, initially empty, how many page faults will FIFO, LRU or Optimal produce?
questions.explanation_en: Each distinct page faults once when it is first referenced (a compulsory fault). With 8 frames all 6 pages fit, so no page is ever replaced and no further faults occur. Every algorithm therefore gives exactly 6 faults.

questions.question_en:
Consider the statements:
I. LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms, so they never show Belady's anomaly.
II. Under FIFO, giving a process more frames can increase its page faults for some reference strings.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.explanation_en: In a stack algorithm the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1 frames, so faults can never rise when frames are added; LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms. FIFO is not, and for strings such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 it gives more faults with more frames. Both statements are correct.

questions.question_en: CPU utilisation is falling, so the long-term scheduler admits more processes; paging activity soars and utilisation falls even further. What is the correct remedy?

options.en: Reduce the size of the swap space
Admit even more processes to the system
Switch from LRU to FIFO replacement

questions.explanation_en: This is thrashing: processes do not have enough frames for their working sets, so they spend more time paging than executing. Admitting more processes makes it worse. Suspending or swapping out some processes (lowering the degree of multiprogramming) frees frames and stops the thrashing.

questions.question_en: With a working-set window Δ = 5, what is the working set just after the last reference of the string 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5?
questions.explanation_en: The working set is the set of distinct pages in the most recent Δ references. The last 5 references are 2, 6, 5, 3, 5, so the working set is {2, 3, 5, 6} and its size is 4. Including 9 would need a window of 6.

tests.title: OS Practice — File Systems & Disk
tests.subject: Computer Science
tests.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which file attribute is a unique tag, usually a number, that identifies the file within the file system and is not meant to be read by humans?
questions.explanation_en: Silberschatz lists file attributes as name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, and time/date/user identification. The identifier is the unique, non-human-readable number (such as an inode number). The name is the human-readable form.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which file operation only sets the current-file-position pointer to a new value, so that no data is actually read from or written to the disk?
questions.explanation_en: Repositioning, also called a file seek, just changes the file-position pointer kept for the open file. It needs no actual I/O. Reading, appending and truncating all access or change the file's data blocks.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Direct (relative) access to a file is based on a ______ model of a file, while sequential access is based on a ______ model.
questions.explanation_en: Sequential access processes records in order, one after another, like a tape. Direct access treats the file as numbered blocks that can be read in any order, which is how a disk works. Databases depend on direct access.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which directory structure allows a file or subdirectory to be shared by appearing in more than one directory, while not allowing cycles?
questions.explanation_en: An acyclic-graph directory lets the same file or subdirectory appear in several directories (through links) but forbids cycles. A tree-structured directory gives each file exactly one parent, so it cannot share. Single-level and two-level directories cannot share either.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: In file-system implementation, which per-volume structure holds the information the system needs to boot an operating system from that volume?
questions.explanation_en: The boot control block (the boot block in UFS, the partition boot sector in NTFS) holds what is needed to boot from that volume; it is empty if the volume has no OS. The volume control block holds block counts and free-space details, and the FCB holds one file's details.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which on-disk structure, called the superblock in UFS, holds the number of blocks in the volume, the block size and the free-block count with free-block pointers?
questions.explanation_en: The volume control block stores per-volume details: number of blocks, block size, free-block count and pointers, and free-FCB count and pointers. In UFS it is the superblock and in NTFS it is stored in the master file table. Booting information is in the boot control block instead.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT stored in a UNIX inode?
questions.explanation_en: An inode (UNIX file control block) stores the file type, owner and group, permissions, size, timestamps, link count and block pointers. The file's name is kept in the directory entry, which maps the name to the inode number. That is why one inode can have several names (hard links).

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which disk-allocation method suffers from external fragmentation and makes it hard for a file to grow beyond its original size?
questions.explanation_en: Contiguous allocation gives each file a run of adjacent blocks. As files come and go, free space breaks into small holes (external fragmentation), and a file cannot grow if the next block is taken. Linked and indexed allocation place blocks anywhere, so they do not suffer from this.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A table at the start of the volume has one entry per disk block, and each entry holds the number of the next block of the file. This method is:
questions.explanation_en: The file-allocation table, used by MS-DOS and FAT32, is a variation of linked allocation. Instead of storing the next-block pointer inside each data block, all the pointers are kept together in a table at the start of the volume, so random access is faster after the table is cached.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which allocation method brings all the pointers of a file together into one block, supporting direct access without external fragmentation?
questions.explanation_en: In indexed allocation each file has an index block whose i-th entry points to the i-th data block. This allows direct access, and since blocks can be anywhere there is no external fragmentation. The cost is the space for the index block, even for tiny files.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: An inode has 10 direct pointers, 1 single-indirect pointer and 1 double-indirect pointer. The block size is 1 KB and each block pointer is 4 bytes. What is the maximum file size?
questions.explanation_en: One 1 KB block holds 1024 / 4 = 256 pointers. Direct = 10 blocks, single indirect = 256 blocks, double indirect = 256 × 256 = 65,536 blocks. Total = 10 + 256 + 65,536 = 65,802 blocks × 1 KB = 65,802 KB.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A free-space bit vector begins 00000000 00110100, where bit 1 means the block is free and blocks are numbered from 0. Which is the first free block?
questions.explanation_en: Scanning from bit 0, the first eight bits are all 0 (allocated), and in the next byte bits 8 and 9 are 0 while bit 10 is 1. So block 10 is the first free block (blocks 10, 11 and 13 are free in this part). A bit vector makes finding the first free block fast.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which technique lets a device controller move a whole block of data directly between the device and main memory, interrupting the CPU only once per block?
questions.explanation_en: With DMA the CPU gives the DMA controller the source, destination and byte count, and the controller transfers the block on its own. The CPU is interrupted only when the whole transfer is complete. Programmed I/O makes the CPU move every byte itself.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which statement about the NTFS file system is FALSE?

options.en: It cannot compress individual files or folders
It describes every file by a record in the MFT
It logs metadata changes in a journal for recovery
It supports access-control lists on files

questions.explanation_en: NTFS has built-in compression of files and folders, so that statement is false. It is a journaling file system, keeps a record for every file in its Master File Table (MFT), and supports access-control lists and encryption.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A user copies a 6 GB video to a USB drive that has 20 GB free, but gets a 'file too large' error. The drive is most likely formatted as:
questions.explanation_en: FAT32 stores the file size in a 32-bit field, so a single file can be at most 4 GB minus 1 byte. NTFS, exFAT and ext4 allow far larger files. Reformatting the drive as exFAT or NTFS would fix the problem.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk rotates at 6000 rpm, has an average seek time of 4 ms and 100 sectors per track. What is the average time to read one sector?
questions.explanation_en: One rotation = 60 / 6000 s = 10 ms, so average rotational latency = 10 / 2 = 5 ms. Transfer time for one sector = 10 ms / 100 = 0.1 ms. Access time = seek + latency + transfer = 4 + 5 + 0.1 = 9.1 ms.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 70 and the request queue (in arrival order) is 45, 130, 12, 160, 88, 25, 110. What is the total head movement under FCFS?

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 70 and the request queue (in arrival order) is 45, 130, 12, 160, 88, 25, 110. What is the total head movement under SSTF?
questions.explanation_en: SSTF always picks the nearest request: 70→88 (18), →110 (22), →130 (20), →160 (30), →45 (115), →25 (20), →12 (13). Total = 238 cylinders. At 70, 88 (18 away) is nearer than 45 (25 away), so the head first moves up.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 70 and the request queue (in arrival order) is 45, 130, 12, 160, 88, 25, 110. The head is moving towards cylinder 0. What is the total head movement under LOOK?
questions.explanation_en: LOOK goes only as far as the last request in each direction: 70→45→25→12 (58), then reverses 12→88→110→130→160 (148). Total = 58 + 148 = 206. SCAN would run on to cylinder 0, giving 70 + 160 = 230.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 100, moving towards higher cylinders, and the request queue is 150, 35, 92, 180, 10, 120, 64. What is the total head movement under SCAN?
questions.explanation_en: SCAN (elevator) moves up to the end of the disk: 100→120→150→180→199 (99), then reverses and serves 92, 64, 35, 10, stopping at 10 (199 − 10 = 189). Total = 99 + 189 = 288. LOOK would turn at 180 and give 250.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 100, moving towards higher cylinders, and the request queue is 150, 35, 92, 180, 10, 120, 64. Under C-SCAN, counting the return sweep from 199 to 0 as head movement, what is the total head movement?
questions.explanation_en: C-SCAN serves only in one direction: 100→120→150→180→199 (99), returns 199→0 (199), then serves 10, 35, 64, 92 going up (92). Total = 99 + 199 + 92 = 390. Without counting the return sweep it would be 191.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: A disk has cylinders 0–199. The head is at cylinder 100, moving towards higher cylinders, and the request queue is 150, 35, 92, 180, 10, 120, 64. Under C-LOOK, counting the jump back as head movement, what is the total head movement?
questions.explanation_en: C-LOOK goes up only to the last request: 100→120→150→180 (80), jumps back to the lowest request 180→10 (170), then serves 35, 64, 92 (82). Total = 80 + 170 + 82 = 332. Without the jump it would be 162.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: What is the main drawback of SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) disk scheduling?

options.en: It serves requests only in arrival order
Requests far from the head may starve
It gives the largest total head movement
It always sweeps to the disk's last cylinder

questions.explanation_en: SSTF keeps serving whichever request is nearest, so it lowers average seek and response time and raises throughput. But a steady stream of nearby requests can keep a far request waiting indefinitely (starvation), and response time varies a lot. Arrival order is FCFS and sweeping to the end is SCAN.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Which RAID level stripes data at block level and spreads the parity blocks across all the disks?
questions.explanation_en: RAID 5 uses block-level striping with distributed parity, so no single parity disk becomes a bottleneck and one disk failure can be survived. RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy, RAID 1 mirrors, and RAID 4 keeps all parity on one dedicated disk.

questions.chapter: OS — File Systems, Disk Scheduling & I/O
questions.question_en: Output from several jobs printing at once is held on disk and sent to the printer one complete job at a time, so their pages do not mix. This is called:
questions.explanation_en: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) keeps a buffer on disk for a device such as a printer, which cannot interleave data from several jobs. Each job's output is stored as a separate file and printed in turn. Caching keeps copies of data for faster access.

tests.title: OS Practice — Linux Commands (Part 1)
tests.subject: Computer Science

questions.question_en: A Linux administrator wants to edit `fstab`, the file that lists which file systems to mount at boot. In which directory is it found?
questions.explanation_en: `/etc` holds the system-wide configuration files, such as `/etc/fstab`, `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/hosts`. `/dev` holds device files, `/boot` holds the kernel and boot-loader files, and `/mnt` is a temporary mount point.

questions.question_en: Commands meant mainly for system administration, such as `fdisk`, `mkfs` and `reboot`, are traditionally kept in:
questions.explanation_en: `/sbin` (system binaries) holds commands used by the administrator to manage and repair the system. `/bin` holds essential commands for all users, such as `ls` and `cp`. `/home` holds users' home directories and `/opt` holds optional add-on software.

questions.question_en: Which directory is not stored on disk but is generated by the kernel in memory, exposing details of running processes and system data such as `cpuinfo` and `meminfo`?
questions.explanation_en: `/proc` is a virtual (pseudo) file system created by the kernel. It has a numbered directory for every running process and files such as `/proc/cpuinfo` and `/proc/meminfo`. `/var` holds variable data such as logs, and `/lib` holds shared libraries.

questions.question_en: Which pairing of a Linux directory and its usual contents is INCORRECT?

options.en: `/tmp` – temporary files, often cleared at reboot

questions.explanation_en: The kernel image (`vmlinuz`) and boot-loader files are kept in `/boot`, not `/var`. `/var` holds variable data such as log files (`/var/log`), mail and spool files. The other three pairings are correct.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is an absolute path name?
questions.explanation_en: An absolute path starts from the root directory `/`, so it means the same file whatever the current directory is. Paths that start with `..`, `.` or a plain name are relative: they are resolved from the current working directory.

questions.question_en: The current directory is `/home/ravi/projects/web`. After running `cd ../..`, what will `pwd` print?
questions.explanation_en: Each `..` moves up one level: the first goes to `/home/ravi/projects` and the second to `/home/ravi`. `pwd` (print working directory) then shows `/home/ravi`. `cd ..` alone would stop at `/home/ravi/projects`.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT a Unix/Linux shell?
questions.explanation_en: Real shells include the Bourne shell (`sh`), Bourne Again shell (`bash`), C shell (`csh`), TENEX C shell (`tcsh`), Korn shell (`ksh`) and Z shell (`zsh`). There is no 'Gamma shell'; it is a made-up distractor.

questions.question_en: When a user is logged in as root (the superuser), which prompt character does bash show by default?
questions.explanation_en: Bash ends its prompt with `#` for the root user and `$` for ordinary users, so you can see at a glance that commands will run with full privileges. `%` is the traditional C-shell prompt and `>` is the continuation prompt (PS2).

questions.question_en: Which command also lists hidden files, whose names begin with a dot?
questions.explanation_en: `ls -a` (all) shows every entry, including hidden ones such as `.bashrc`, `.` and `..`. `ls -l` gives a long listing, `ls -R` lists subdirectories recursively and `ls -t` sorts by modification time.

questions.question_en: In `ls -l` output, a line that begins with `lrwxrwxrwx` describes a:
questions.explanation_en: The first character of `ls -l` output is the file type: `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link, `c` character device, `b` block device. So `l` means a symbolic (soft) link; a symlink always shows `rwxrwxrwx`.

questions.question_en: Which command renames `old.txt` to `new.txt` in the same directory?
questions.explanation_en: `mv` both moves and renames files; renaming is just moving to a new name in the same directory. `cp` would leave the old file in place, `ln` makes a hard link (two names), and `ren` is a DOS/Windows command, not a Linux one.

questions.question_en: Which option makes `rm` ask for confirmation before deleting each file?
questions.explanation_en: `rm -i` (interactive) prompts before every removal. `-f` (force) never prompts and ignores missing files, `-r` removes directories recursively and `-v` (verbose) prints the name of each file removed.

questions.question_en: `rmdir project` fails with the message 'Directory not empty'. Which command deletes `project` together with everything inside it?
questions.explanation_en: `rmdir` removes only empty directories. `rm -r` (recursive) deletes a directory and all its files and subdirectories. Plain `rm project` refuses because it is a directory, `rmdir` has no `-f` option, and `del` is not a Linux command.

questions.question_en: Which command creates the directory path `a/b/c` in one step even though `a` and `a/b` do not exist yet?
questions.explanation_en: `mkdir -p` (parents) creates any missing parent directories and gives no error if they already exist. Plain `mkdir a/b/c` fails because `a/b` is missing. `mkdir` has no `-r` or `-a` option.

questions.question_en: If `report.txt` does not exist, what does `touch report.txt` do?
questions.explanation_en: `touch` updates a file's access and modification times; if the file does not exist it creates it as an empty file. It is the usual quick way to create a blank file. It never opens an editor or prints contents.

questions.question_en: A hard link is made with `ln data.txt copy.txt`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.en: Both names share one inode, so the data stays if `data.txt` is deleted
It makes a separate, independent copy of the data
It stores only the path, so it breaks if `data.txt` is deleted
It can point to a file on a different file system

questions.explanation_en: A hard link is a second directory entry pointing to the same inode, and the link count rises to 2. Deleting one name only lowers the count; the data stays until the count reaches 0. Storing a path and breaking on deletion describes a symbolic link (`ln -s`), and hard links cannot cross file systems.

questions.question_en: Which command prints the lines of `access.log` that do NOT contain the word `error`?
questions.explanation_en: `grep` prints lines that match a pattern, and `-v` inverts the match so non-matching lines are printed. `-i` ignores case, `-c` prints only the count of matching lines and `-n` adds line numbers.

questions.question_en: What does `grep -c "Delhi" cities.txt` print?

options.en: The names of files that contain Delhi
Every line that does not contain Delhi
Each line containing Delhi with its line number
The number of lines that contain Delhi

questions.explanation_en: `-c` (count) makes `grep` print only how many lines match, not the lines themselves. Line numbers come from `-n`, non-matching lines from `-v`, and file names only from `-l`.

questions.question_en: Which command searches `/home` and all its subdirectories for files whose names end in `.pdf`?
questions.explanation_en: `find` walks a directory tree and tests each file; `-name "*.pdf"` matches names ending in .pdf. The pattern is quoted so the shell does not expand it first. `grep` searches inside file contents, and `which` finds the path of an executable command.

questions.question_en: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x--x` for a file. What is its permission in octal?
questions.explanation_en: Split into owner `rwx`, group `r-x` and others `--x`. With r = 4, w = 2, x = 1: owner 4+2+1 = 7, group 4+0+1 = 5, others 0+0+1 = 1. So the mode is 751.

questions.question_en: After `chmod 640 salary.xls`, which permission string does `ls -l` show?
questions.explanation_en: 6 = 4 + 2 = `rw-` for the owner, 4 = `r--` for the group and 0 = `---` for others, giving `-rw-r-----`. `-rw-r--r--` would be 644 and `-rwxr-----` would be 740.

questions.question_en: A file has permissions `rw-rw-rw-`. What are its permissions after `chmod go-w file`?
questions.explanation_en: In symbolic mode `g` is the group, `o` is others and `-w` removes write permission. The owner is untouched, so the result is `rw-r--r--` (644). `rw-------` would need `go-rw`.

questions.question_en: Which of these is a correctly formed command to give the owner execute permission on `backup.sh`?
questions.explanation_en: `chmod` takes two arguments in this order: the permission change, then the file name(s). The change is written as who (`u`, `g`, `o`, `a`), an operator (`+`, `-`, `=`) and the permissions (`r`, `w`, `x`), or as an octal number such as 755.

questions.question_en: With the common umask of `022`, a user creates `notes.txt` with a text editor. What permissions does the new file get?
questions.explanation_en: New regular files start from 666 (no execute bit), and the umask switches off the bits it contains (mode AND NOT umask): 666 masked by 022 = 644 = `rw-r--r--`. Directories start from 777 and so get 755. Text files never get execute permission by default.

questions.question_en: A user runs `umask 027` and then `mkdir reports`. What are the permissions of `reports`?
questions.explanation_en: Directories start from 777, and the umask switches off the bits it contains (mode AND NOT umask). 027 removes write for the group and all permissions for others: 777 masked by 027 = 750 = `rwxr-x---`. A regular file created with the same umask would get 666 masked by 027 = 640 (`rw-r-----`); note this is a bit mask, not ordinary subtraction.

questions.question_en: Which command makes user `meena` the owner of `plan.doc`?
questions.explanation_en: `chown` (change owner) sets a file's owner, and `chown meena:staff plan.doc` can set the group too. `chgrp` changes only the group, `chmod` changes permissions, and `useradd` creates a new user account.

questions.question_en: `ls -ld /tmp` shows `drwxrwxrwt`. What does the final `t` mean?

options.en: Trusted flag: only root may create files there
Temporary flag: files are deleted every hour
SUID bit: programs run with the owner's rights
Sticky bit: users can delete only their own files there

questions.explanation_en: A `t` in the others-execute position is the sticky bit (octal 1000, as in `chmod 1777 /tmp`). In a world-writable directory it lets every user create files but allows only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root to delete or rename a file. SUID shows as `s` in the owner's execute position.

questions.question_en: Which command sets the SUID bit together with `rwxr-xr-x` permissions on `myprog`?
questions.explanation_en: The leading octal digit sets the special bits: 4 = SUID, 2 = SGID, 1 = sticky. So 4755 gives `rwsr-xr-x`, and the program runs with its owner's privileges, as `/usr/bin/passwd` does. 2755 sets SGID and 1755 sets the sticky bit.

questions.question_en: Which command shows a continuously refreshing, real-time list of processes sorted by CPU usage?
questions.explanation_en: `top` displays a live view of running processes, refreshing every few seconds with CPU and memory usage. `ps` prints a one-time snapshot, `jobs` lists only the current shell's jobs, and `pwd` prints the working directory.

questions.question_en: What does `kill -9 4321` do?

options.en: Pauses process 4321 for nine seconds, then resumes it
Sends SIGTERM to process 4321, asking it to exit cleanly
Sends SIGKILL to process 4321, which it cannot catch or ignore
Kills nine processes, starting from process ID 4321

questions.explanation_en: Signal 9 is SIGKILL: the kernel ends the process at once and the process cannot catch, block or ignore it. Plain `kill 4321` sends signal 15, SIGTERM, which lets the process clean up first. `kill` takes a signal and process IDs, not a count.

questions.question_en: A long-running command was paused with Ctrl+Z. Which command resumes it in the background so that the prompt stays free?
questions.explanation_en: Ctrl+Z stops the foreground job. `bg` continues it in the background, just as if it had been started with `&`. `fg` would bring it back to the foreground, `jobs` only lists the jobs, and `nice` sets the priority of a new command.

questions.question_en: Which command reports the used and available space on each mounted file system?
questions.explanation_en: `df` (disk free) lists every mounted file system with its size, used and available space; `-h` prints sizes like 20G. `du` shows the space used by particular files and directories, `free` shows RAM and swap, and `uname -a` shows system and kernel information.

questions.question_en: What does `rm *log` do in the current directory?

options.en: Deletes only a file literally named `*log`
Deletes every file whose name begins with `log`
Lists every file whose name ends with `log`
Deletes every file whose name ends with `log`

questions.explanation_en: The shell expands `*log` to all names that end in `log` (the `*` matches any characters, including none, but not a leading dot, so hidden files are skipped), and `rm` deletes those files. Names beginning with `log` would need `log*`, and listing would need `ls`, not `rm`.

questions.question_en: What does `tar -xzvf site.tar.gz` do?

options.en: Extracts the gzip-compressed archive, listing each file
Lists the archive's contents without extracting them

questions.explanation_en: `-x` extracts, `-z` filters through gzip, `-v` (verbose) lists each file and `-f` names the archive file. Creating an archive would use `-c` (as in `tar -czvf`), and only listing would use `-t`.

questions.question_en:
What does `out.txt` contain after these commands run?
```bash
echo "one" > out.txt
echo "two" >> out.txt
echo "three" > out.txt
```
questions.explanation_en: `>` creates or overwrites a file, while `>>` appends to it. After the first two commands the file holds `one` and `two`, but the third command uses `>` again, which empties the file before writing. So only `three` is left.

tests.description: 35 most expected questions on Linux / Unix Commands & Shell, with solutions.

tests.title: OS Practice — Linux Commands (Part 2)
tests.subject: Computer Science

questions.question_en: In `ls /data 2> err.txt`, what is written to `err.txt`?

options.en: Both the listing and the error messages
Only the exit status of the ls command

questions.explanation_en: File descriptor 2 is standard error, so `2>` redirects only error messages into `err.txt`, while the normal listing still appears on the screen. Both together would need `> file 2>&1` or `&> file`.

questions.question_en: What does `sort names.txt | head -n 3` display?

options.en: The first three lines of the file, unsorted
The last three names in sorted order
Only the first three lines are sorted, the rest not
The first three names in sorted order

questions.explanation_en: The pipe `|` sends the output of `sort` as the input of `head`. `sort` puts all names in order and `head -n 3` keeps only the first three lines of that sorted output. The file itself is not changed.

questions.question_en: A directory contains `f1.c`, `f12.c`, `fa.c` and `f.c`. Which files does `ls f?.c` list?
questions.explanation_en: The `?` wildcard matches exactly one character. `f1.c` and `fa.c` have one character between `f` and `.c`; `f12.c` has two and `f.c` has none. `f*.c` would match all four.

questions.question_en: In `mkdir backup && cp *.txt backup`, when does the `cp` command run?

options.en: At the same time as `mkdir`, in the background

questions.explanation_en: `&&` runs the second command only if the first one succeeds. `||` runs it only if the first fails, `;` runs it in any case, and `&` puts a command in the background.

questions.question_en: In the vi editor, which command quits WITHOUT saving the changes?
questions.explanation_en: In command mode, `:q!` quits and throws away unsaved changes. `:wq` and `ZZ` both save and then quit, and `:w` saves without quitting. Press Esc first to leave insert mode.

questions.question_en:
What is printed when this script is run as `./show.sh red green blue`?
```bash
#!/bin/bash
echo "$# $1"
```
questions.explanation_en: `$#` holds the number of command-line arguments (3: red, green, blue) and `$1` holds the first argument (red). The script name is `$0` and is not counted in `$#`. So the output is `3 red`.

questions.question_en: Right after a command finishes, what does `echo $?` print?

options.en: The exit status of that command (0 = success)
The number of arguments given to it
The process ID of the current shell
The name of the current shell script

questions.explanation_en: `$?` holds the exit status of the last command: 0 means success and any other value means an error. The shell's process ID is `$$`, the number of arguments is `$#` and the script name is `$0`.

questions.question_en: The first line `#!/bin/bash` in a shell script is used to:

options.en: Run the script with root privileges
Mark the whole script as a comment block
Name the interpreter that should run the script

questions.explanation_en: The `#!` line (shebang) tells the kernel which program should run the script, here `/bin/bash`. Execute permission must still be given separately with `chmod +x`. To the shell itself, the line is just a comment.

questions.question_en: Most current Linux distributions, such as Ubuntu and Debian, format the root partition by default with:
questions.explanation_en: ext4 (fourth extended file system) is the default on most distributions. It is a journaling file system with extents and support for very large files and volumes. ext2 had no journal, and NTFS and FAT32 are Windows file systems.

questions.question_en:
What does this bash snippet print?
```bash
a=7
b=3
echo $((a % b + a / b))
```
questions.explanation_en: Bash `$(( ))` does integer arithmetic. `a % b` = 7 mod 3 = 1, and `a / b` = 7 / 3 = 2 because the fraction is dropped. So the result is 1 + 2 = 3.

tests.title: OS — 200 Most Expected Questions (Full Test)
tests.subject: Computer Science

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: According to Silberschatz–Galvin, an operating system is best described as:

options.en: a program that translates high-level source code into equivalent machine code before execution
a program that acts as an intermediary between the user of a computer and the computer hardware
a hardware unit that permanently stores the data and instructions needed by the processor
a utility program whose only job is to organise the files stored on a hard disk

questions.explanation_en: An operating system is a program that manages the computer hardware and acts as an intermediary (interface/bridge) between the user and the hardware. Translating source code is the job of a compiler, which is a system program, not the OS itself.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: The one program that runs at all times on the computer, usually called the core of the operating system, is the ______.
questions.explanation_en: Silberschatz defines the kernel as "the one program running at all times on the computer". The shell is only a command interpreter, and the bootstrap loader runs only at start-up to load the kernel.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: In the simple probabilistic model of multiprogramming, each process spends a fraction p of its time waiting for I/O, so CPU utilisation = 1 − pⁿ for n processes in memory. If every process waits for I/O 80% of the time and 3 processes are in memory, the CPU utilisation is about:
questions.explanation_en: The CPU is idle only when all 3 processes are waiting for I/O at the same time, with probability 0.8³ = 0.512. So utilisation = 1 − 0.512 = 0.488, i.e. about 48.8%. The value 51.2% is the idle fraction, not the utilisation.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: In a batch operating system:

options.en: each user interacts directly with the program while it is running
jobs with similar needs are grouped together and run without user interaction
every task must finish within a strict, fixed deadline or it fails
processing is shared among many computers linked by a network

questions.explanation_en: A batch system collects jobs with similar requirements into batches and runs them one after another with no interaction between the user and the job while it runs. Interaction is a feature of time-sharing, deadlines of real-time systems, and networked processing of distributed systems.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Time sharing (multitasking) is a logical extension of ______, in which the CPU switches among jobs so frequently that users can interact with each program while it is running.
questions.explanation_en: Silberschatz describes time sharing as a logical extension of multiprogramming. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory to keep the CPU busy; time sharing adds very frequent switching so that each user gets a quick, interactive response.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: The main objective of multiprogramming is to:

options.en: allow a single user to run exactly one program at any given time
guarantee that every process meets a strict and fixed deadline
connect several computers so that they share one common clock
increase CPU utilisation by always keeping a job for the CPU to execute

questions.explanation_en: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory; when one job has to wait (for example for I/O), the OS switches the CPU to another job. Thus the CPU is never idle as long as some job needs to execute, which increases CPU utilisation.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Which of the following statements about real-time systems is correct?

options.en: A soft real-time system guarantees critical tasks finish on time; a hard one only gives them priority
A hard real-time system guarantees critical tasks finish on time; a soft one only gives them priority
Both hard and soft real-time systems allow a critical deadline to be missed now and then
Real-time systems are meant only for batch jobs that have no time limits of any kind

questions.explanation_en: A hard real-time system guarantees that critical real-time tasks are completed within their deadlines; a missed deadline is a system failure. A soft real-time system only gives critical tasks priority over other tasks and retains that priority until they complete, so an occasional missed deadline is tolerable.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Which of the following is the BEST example of a soft real-time system?
questions.explanation_en: In multimedia streaming an occasional late frame only lowers quality, so it is a soft real-time application. Air-bag control, robot-arm control and missile guidance must meet every deadline, so they are hard real-time systems.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: A distributed operating system is best characterised as one in which:

options.en: two or more processors share one memory and one clock inside a single computer
physically separate computers, each with its own memory, cooperate over a network
jobs are collected on tape and processed one batch at a time without interaction
a single CPU switches rapidly between several interactive users at terminals

questions.explanation_en: A distributed system is a collection of physically separate, possibly heterogeneous computer systems, each with its own local memory, networked to give users access to shared resources. Sharing one memory and clock describes a tightly coupled multiprocessor system instead.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en:
Match List I with List II:
List I | List II
I. Asymmetric multiprocessing | 1. Each processor performs all tasks, including operating-system functions
II. Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) | 2. A boss processor schedules and allocates work to worker processors
III. Graceful degradation | 3. Service continues in proportion to the level of surviving hardware
IV. Clustered system | 4. Separate systems joined by a LAN that typically share storage
questions.explanation_en: Asymmetric multiprocessing uses a boss–worker relationship, while in SMP every processor is a peer that performs all tasks. Graceful degradation is the ability to keep providing service proportional to the surviving hardware, and a clustered system joins separate computers, usually over a LAN with shared storage.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: In dual-mode operation, the hardware mode bit indicates the current mode. Its value is:

options.en: 1 for kernel mode and 0 for user mode
0 for kernel mode and 1 for user mode
0 for both kernel mode and user mode
1 for both kernel mode and user mode

questions.explanation_en: A mode bit is added to the hardware: kernel (supervisor/privileged) mode = 0 and user mode = 1. On a trap or interrupt the hardware switches from user mode to kernel mode by setting the bit to 0, and the OS sets it back to 1 before passing control to a user program.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Which of the following instructions need NOT be privileged?

options.en: Set the value of the timer
Issue direct I/O to a device

questions.explanation_en: Instructions that could harm the system—setting the timer, disabling interrupts, performing I/O directly—are privileged and can run only in kernel mode. Merely reading the clock cannot damage the system or other users, so it can safely be executed in user mode.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: A software-generated interrupt, caused either by an error (such as division by zero) or by a specific request from a user program for an operating-system service, is called a(n):
questions.explanation_en: A trap or exception is a software-generated interrupt caused by an error or by a user program requesting an OS service (a system call). Hardware interrupts come from devices through signals to the CPU, and DMA is a way for devices to move data without the CPU.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Silberschatz divides OS services into those that help the user and those that ensure the efficient operation of the system itself. Which service belongs to the SECOND group?
questions.explanation_en: Services for the user include the user interface, program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communications and error detection. Services for efficient operation of the system itself are resource allocation, logging (accounting), and protection and security.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT a service provided by an operating system?

options.en: Detecting errors in hardware and in programs
Loading programs into memory and running them
Performing I/O operations requested by programs
Correcting the logical errors in a user's algorithm

questions.explanation_en: Error detection, program execution and I/O operations are standard OS services. The OS can report run-time errors, but finding and correcting logic errors in an algorithm is the programmer's job, not a service of the operating system.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: System calls provide:

options.en: a method for the compiler to optimise the loops in source code
a hardware path that bypasses the CPU for all disk transfers
a record of the commands a user has typed at the shell prompt
an interface to the services made available by an operating system

questions.explanation_en: System calls provide an interface to the services made available by the operating system; they are the way a running program requests a service from the kernel. They are usually reached through an API such as POSIX or the Windows API.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en:
Match the system calls (List I) with their category (List II):
List I | List II
I. wait event, signal event | 1. File management
II. open, close, read, write | 2. Information maintenance
III. get time or date, set system data | 3. Communications
IV. send, receive messages | 4. Process control
questions.explanation_en: In Silberschatz's list, wait event/signal event are process-control calls, and open/close/read/write are file-management calls. Get time or date and set system data are information-maintenance calls, while send/receive messages are communication calls.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: In Silberschatz's classification, the system calls "create, delete communication connection" and "attach or detach remote devices" belong to which category?
questions.explanation_en: The communications category contains create/delete communication connection, send/receive messages, transfer status information, and attach or detach remote devices. Device management covers local calls such as request/release device and read/write/reposition.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: The system calls "allocate and free memory" and "wait for time" fall under which category of system calls?
questions.explanation_en: Process-control calls include end/abort, load/execute, create/terminate process, get/set process attributes, wait for time, wait event/signal event, and allocate and free memory. Information maintenance only gets or sets data such as the time, date or system data.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT a general method of passing parameters to the operating system during a system call?

options.en: Storing them in a memory block and passing its address
Embedding them in the interrupt vector table

questions.explanation_en: Silberschatz lists three methods: pass the parameters in registers, store them in a block or table in memory and pass the block's address in a register, or push them onto the stack for the OS to pop. The interrupt vector only holds addresses of interrupt service routines, not call parameters.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Which of the following statements about a microkernel is TRUE?

options.en: All operating-system services run together in one large kernel address space
It is faster than a monolithic kernel because it never has to pass messages
Most services run as user-level processes that communicate by message passing
Adding any new service always requires modifying and rebuilding the kernel

questions.explanation_en: A microkernel keeps only minimal functions (process and memory management, communication) in the kernel and moves other services to user space, where they communicate through message passing. This makes it small, easy to extend and more reliable, but the message-passing overhead makes it slower than a monolithic kernel, which runs everything in a single address space.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: In the layered approach to OS design, layer 0 is the hardware and the highest layer is the user interface. The main advantage of this approach is:

options.en: no need to decide carefully what goes in each layer
freedom for any layer to call the layers above it

questions.explanation_en: Each layer uses only the functions and services of lower layers, so layers can be built and debugged one at a time—this simplicity of construction and debugging is the main advantage. The drawbacks are the difficulty of defining the layers properly and lower performance, since a request may have to pass through several layers.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: Modern kernels such as Linux and Solaris link in additional services (for example, device drivers and file systems) at boot time or run time through:
questions.explanation_en: The modular approach uses loadable kernel modules: the kernel has a set of core components and links in additional services dynamically. It is like a layered system in having defined interfaces, but more flexible because any module can call any other module.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: The small program that runs when the computer is powered on, initialises the system and loads the operating-system kernel into memory, and is usually stored in ROM or EEPROM (firmware), is the:
questions.explanation_en: Booting is starting a computer by loading the kernel. The bootstrap program (bootstrap loader), kept in firmware, initialises CPU registers, device controllers and memory, then locates the kernel, loads it into main memory and starts its execution.

questions.chapter: OS — Introduction, OS Structure & System Calls
questions.question_en: The UNIX operating system was originally developed at Bell Labs by:
questions.explanation_en: UNIX was developed at AT&T Bell Labs around 1969–1970 by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, and Ritchie's C language was later used to rewrite it. Linus Torvalds created the Linux kernel in 1991, and Tanenbaum wrote the MINIX teaching OS.

questions.question_en: A program is a ______ entity, whereas a process is an ______ entity.
questions.explanation_en: A program is a passive entity, such as a file containing a list of instructions stored on disk. A process is an active entity—a program in execution with a program counter and a set of associated resources; a program becomes a process when it is loaded into memory.

questions.question_en: Which section of a process in memory holds memory that is dynamically allocated during run time, for example by malloc()?
questions.explanation_en: A process in memory has a text section (code), a data section (global variables), a heap (memory dynamically allocated at run time) and a stack (temporary data such as function parameters, return addresses and local variables). The heap and stack grow towards each other.

questions.question_en:
Match the process states with their meanings:
State | Meaning
I. Waiting | 1. The process has finished execution
II. Ready | 2. The process is waiting for some event, such as I/O completion
III. Terminated | 3. The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor
IV. Running | 4. Instructions are being executed
questions.explanation_en: Waiting means the process waits for an event (such as I/O completion or a signal); Ready means it waits only for the CPU. Terminated means it has finished execution, and Running means its instructions are being executed.

questions.question_en: Which of the following state transitions is NOT possible in the standard five-state process model?
questions.explanation_en: When the event a waiting process needs occurs, it goes to the Ready state; it must then be selected by the scheduler before it can run. So Waiting → Running directly is not allowed, while Running → Waiting (I/O request), Waiting → Ready (event completes) and Ready → Running (dispatch) are normal transitions.

questions.question_en: A running process is moved back to the ready state when:

options.en: it issues an I/O request and must wait for the device
a timer interrupt occurs because its time slice has expired
it executes its last statement and calls exit()
the I/O operation it was waiting for is completed

questions.explanation_en: An interrupt (such as the timer ending the time quantum) moves a process from Running to Ready. An I/O request moves it from Running to Waiting, exit() moves it to Terminated, and I/O completion moves a Waiting process to Ready.

questions.question_en:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: A process moves from the waiting state to the ready state when the event it was waiting for occurs.
Statement II: All the memory allocated to a process is reclaimed by the operating system when the process terminates.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_en: Statement I is correct: on I/O or event completion a waiting process becomes ready, not running. Statement II is also correct: when a process terminates (for example by calling exit()), all its resources—physical and virtual memory, open files and I/O buffers—are deallocated by the operating system.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT normally stored in a process control block (PCB)?

options.en: The program counter and the CPU register contents
CPU-scheduling information such as process priority
The source code from which the program was compiled
Memory-management information such as page tables

questions.explanation_en: The PCB stores the process state, program counter, CPU registers, CPU-scheduling information, memory-management information, accounting information and I/O status information (such as open files). The source code of the program is not part of a running process's PCB.

questions.question_en: Which of the following statements about context switching is correct?

options.en: The system performs useful user work while the switch is in progress
The state of the old process is discarded instead of being saved
Its speed depends on hardware support, such as multiple sets of registers
It is carried out by the long-term scheduler when a job is admitted

questions.explanation_en: During a context switch the kernel saves the state of the old process in its PCB and loads the saved state of the new one; this time is pure overhead because no useful work is done. Context-switch time depends heavily on hardware support—some processors provide multiple register sets, so a switch just changes a pointer.

questions.question_en: The ______ scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming, that is, the number of processes in memory.
questions.explanation_en: The long-term (job) scheduler selects processes from the job pool on disk and loads them into memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming. The short-term (CPU) scheduler only picks which ready process gets the CPU next.

questions.question_en: Removing a process from memory to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, and later bringing it back so that it continues where it left off, is called ______ and is done by the ______ scheduler.
questions.explanation_en: The medium-term scheduler swaps a process out of memory (and later swaps it back in) to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or to improve the process mix. Swapping may also be needed when memory becomes over-committed.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT a function of the dispatcher?

options.en: Switching context from one process to another process
Switching the CPU from kernel mode to user mode
Jumping to the proper location in the user program to restart it
Selecting which new jobs are admitted into memory from the job pool

questions.explanation_en: The dispatcher is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler: it switches context, switches to user mode and jumps to the proper location in the user program. Admitting new jobs is done by the long-term scheduler. The time the dispatcher takes is called dispatch latency.

questions.question_en: After a successful fork() call, the value returned to the child process is ______ and the value returned to the parent process is ______.
questions.explanation_en: fork() creates a new process that is a copy of the parent and returns twice: 0 in the child and the (non-zero) process identifier of the new child in the parent. A negative value is returned to the parent only if the fork fails.

questions.question_en: Which statement about the exec() family of system calls (for example execlp()) is correct?

options.en: It replaces the calling process's memory image with a new program
It creates a new child process that is a copy of its parent
It makes the parent wait until one of its children terminates
It returns the PID of the newly loaded program to its caller

questions.explanation_en: exec() loads a binary file into memory, destroying the memory image of the program that called it, and starts its execution; the PID stays the same. On success it does not return at all. Creating a copy is done by fork(), and waiting for a child is done by wait().

questions.question_en: A parent process calls wait(). Which of the following is correct?

options.en: It immediately terminates all of the parent's child processes
It makes the child wait until the parent process terminates
It blocks until a child terminates and then returns that child's PID
It loads a new program into the parent's own address space

questions.explanation_en: wait() suspends the parent until one of its children terminates; it returns the PID of the terminated child and can collect the child's exit status. This also removes the child's entry from the process table, so it no longer remains a zombie.

questions.question_en: A process that has terminated but whose parent has not yet called wait() to collect its exit status is called a(n):
questions.explanation_en: When a process terminates, its entry in the process table stays until the parent calls wait(), because the table holds its exit status. During this period the process is a zombie; once the parent calls wait(), its PID and table entry are released.

questions.question_en: If a parent process terminates without calling wait(), its still-running children become ______ and, in traditional UNIX, are adopted by ______.

options.en: zombies; the login shell of the user

questions.explanation_en: Children whose parent has terminated without invoking wait() are orphans. Traditional UNIX makes the init process (systemd on modern Linux) their new parent; init calls wait() periodically, which collects their exit status and releases their process-table entries.

Each fork() doubles the number of processes: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. All 8 processes (the original plus 7 children) reach printf(), so "OS" is printed 2³ = 8 times. In general n unconditional forks give 2ⁿ processes and 2ⁿ − 1 children.

The printf() is inside the loop, so it runs after each fork. In iteration 0 there are 2 processes (2 prints), in iteration 1 there are 4 (4 prints) and in iteration 2 there are 8 (8 prints). Total = 2 + 4 + 8 = 14.

The parent gets a non-zero value from the first fork, so || short-circuits, the condition is true and it forks again: 2 prints. The first child gets 0, so it evaluates the second fork; it receives a non-zero value, forks once more and gives 2 prints, while the grandchild created by the second fork gets 0 (condition false) and prints once. Total = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

Each child gets 0 from fork() and immediately breaks out of the loop, so children never create further processes. Only the original parent keeps looping and creates 4 children in total. The parent and its 4 children each print once: 5 times.

After fork() the child gets its own copy of the address space, so changing x in the child does not affect the parent's x. The parent waits for the child, so the child prints 5 + 10 = 15 first; then the parent prints its own 5 − 2 = 3.

questions.question_en: In the fork–join construct for concurrent programming, the join instruction is used to:

options.en: split one computation into two computations that run in parallel
move a process from the ready queue to the running state
recombine two or more concurrent computations into a single one
permanently delete the PCB of a process that has finished

questions.explanation_en: fork splits a single computation into two concurrent computations, and join recombines concurrent computations into one—the computation after join continues only when all the joined branches have finished. Used together, fork and join express a complete concurrent subroutine.

questions.question_en: Which statement comparing shared memory and message passing for interprocess communication is correct?

options.en: Shared memory needs system calls only to set up the region; message passing usually needs one per message
Message passing is always faster than shared memory because it never involves the kernel at all
Shared memory cannot be used by cooperating processes that run on the same computer system
With shared memory the kernel must copy every byte that one process sends to the other one

questions.explanation_en: In shared memory, system calls are needed only to establish the shared region; after that, accesses are ordinary memory accesses with no kernel help, so it can be faster. Message passing is typically implemented with system calls (kernel intervention) for each send and receive, but it is easier to implement and is useful for smaller amounts of data and in distributed systems.

questions.question_en: A socket, used for communication between processes over a network, is defined as:

options.en: a pipe that can be shared only between a parent and its child process
an endpoint for communication, identified by an IP address and a port number
a block of memory shared by cooperating processes on a single machine
a signal that notifies a process that a particular event has happened

questions.explanation_en: A socket is defined as an endpoint for communication; a pair of processes communicating over a network uses a pair of sockets, one per process. A socket is identified by an IP address concatenated with a port number, for example 161.25.19.8:1625.

questions.question_en: Which of the following statements about pipes is correct?

options.en: An ordinary pipe is two-way and can be used by any unrelated processes on the system
An ordinary pipe is one-way and needs a parent–child relationship; a named pipe does not
A named pipe (FIFO) ceases to exist as soon as the process that created it terminates
Pipes can be used only between processes running on different computers in a network

questions.explanation_en: An ordinary (anonymous) pipe allows one-way, producer–consumer communication and requires a parent–child relationship; it exists only while the processes use it. A named pipe (FIFO) appears in the file system, needs no parent–child relationship, and continues to exist after the communicating processes have finished.

questions.question_en: Which signal in UNIX/Linux can be neither caught nor ignored by a process?
questions.explanation_en: A signal notifies a process that a particular event has occurred, and most signals can be handled by a user-defined handler or ignored. SIGKILL (signal 9, sent by kill -9) and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so SIGKILL always terminates the process.

questions.question_en: Threads that belong to the same process share which of the following?

options.en: Stack, register set and program counter
Thread ID and its own private stack
Program counter and the data section only
Code section, data section and open files

questions.explanation_en: A thread is a basic unit of CPU utilisation with its own thread ID, program counter, register set and stack. It shares with the other threads of the same process its code section, data section and other OS resources such as open files and signals.

questions.question_en: Which of the following is NOT one of the benefits of multithreaded programming listed by Silberschatz?
questions.explanation_en: The four benefits are responsiveness, resource sharing, economy (threads are cheaper to create and switch than processes) and scalability on multicore systems. Because threads share data, multithreaded programs are actually more prone to race conditions and need synchronisation.

questions.question_en: In the many-to-one multithreading model:

options.en: threads of one process can run in parallel on several cores
each user thread is mapped to its own separate kernel thread
a blocking system call by one thread blocks the entire process
the kernel schedules every user thread of a process separately

questions.explanation_en: The many-to-one model maps many user-level threads to a single kernel thread; thread management is done by a user-space library. Because only one thread can access the kernel at a time, a blocking system call blocks the whole process, and the threads cannot run in parallel on multicore systems.

questions.question_en: Modern Linux and Windows operating systems implement which multithreading model?
questions.explanation_en: Linux and the Windows family use the one-to-one model, which maps each user thread to a kernel thread. This allows more concurrency (another thread can run when one blocks) and parallelism on multiprocessors; the cost is creating a kernel thread for every user thread.

questions.question_en: Which of the following definitions is CORRECT?

options.en: Response time: time from submission of a request until the first response is produced
Waiting time: total time from the arrival of a process until its completion
Turnaround time: time a process spends waiting only in the ready queue
Burst time: time a process waits before it gets the CPU for the first time

questions.explanation_en: Response time is the time from submission of a request until the first response is produced. Waiting time is the total time spent waiting in the ready queue, turnaround time is completion time − arrival time, and burst time is the CPU time the process needs to execute.

questions.question_en: A CPU-scheduling algorithm is considered better if it:

options.en: maximises waiting time and turnaround time and minimises throughput
maximises turnaround time and minimises CPU utilisation and throughput
minimises CPU utilisation and throughput and maximises response time
maximises CPU utilisation and throughput and minimises waiting time

questions.explanation_en: It is desirable to maximise CPU utilisation and throughput (number of processes completed per time unit) and to minimise turnaround time, waiting time and response time. Hence a good scheduler has high throughput and low turnaround time.

questions.question_en: CPU-scheduling decisions may take place when a process (1) switches from running to waiting, (2) switches from running to ready, (3) switches from waiting to ready, or (4) terminates. Scheduling is non-preemptive (cooperative) when decisions are made only under:
questions.explanation_en: In circumstances 1 and 4 there is no choice—a new process must be selected because the running process has given up the CPU. If scheduling happens only then, it is non-preemptive: a process keeps the CPU until it terminates or switches to waiting. Scheduling under circumstances 2 and 3 as well is preemptive.

questions.question_en: Which of the following scheduling algorithms is inherently non-preemptive?
questions.explanation_en: Under FCFS, once the CPU is allocated to a process, the process keeps it until it terminates or requests I/O, so FCFS is non-preemptive. RR, SRTF and preemptive priority scheduling all take the CPU away from a running process.

questions.question_en: SJF scheduling is provably optimal because it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes. Its main practical difficulty is that:

options.en: it needs a time quantum that is very hard to choose well
it cannot be used when all the jobs arrive at the same time
it always causes the convoy effect for the short processes
the length of the next CPU burst is not known in advance

questions.explanation_en: The real difficulty with SJF is knowing the length of the next CPU request. For short-term scheduling it can only be approximated—typically by predicting the next burst as an exponential average of the measured lengths of previous bursts.

questions.question_en: The convoy effect, in which many short processes wait for one long CPU-bound process to release the CPU, is associated with which scheduling algorithm?
questions.explanation_en: Under FCFS, if a big CPU-bound process gets the CPU, all the short I/O-bound processes pile up behind it, which lowers CPU and device utilisation. This is the convoy effect; preemptive algorithms such as SRTF and RR avoid it.

questions.question_en: Gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time, so that they are not blocked indefinitely, is called:
questions.explanation_en: Priority scheduling can cause indefinite blocking (starvation) of low-priority processes. Aging solves this by slowly raising the priority of a waiting process—for example by 1 every 15 minutes—so it eventually gets the highest priority and runs.

questions.question_en: In Round Robin scheduling, if the time quantum is made extremely large, the policy behaves like ______; if it is made extremely small, ______.

options.en: FCFS; context-switch overhead becomes very large
SRTF; response time becomes very poor

questions.explanation_en: If the quantum is larger than every CPU burst, no process is ever preempted, so RR becomes FCFS. If it is extremely small, the CPU spends a large share of its time context switching, so the quantum should be large compared with the context-switch time (rule of thumb: about 80% of CPU bursts shorter than the quantum).

questions.question_en: The key difference between multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) scheduling and multilevel queue (MLQ) scheduling is that in MLFQ:
